Try2Fly

We are Try2Fly, a game development team consisting of Miras, Daniyar and Tamerlan. We are passionate game developers who love turning creative ideas into engaging gaming experiences. We combine creativity, technical skills, and a passion for gaming to bring our ideas to life. We are always learning, experimenting, and pushing our limits to create unique and exciting games. Our goal is simple: make great games and have fun doing it!
summary: Mission Forge is a free browser game where players design a real kind of space mission, launch it and find out why it worked or didn’t. Students pick a customer brief (spot wildfires, map lunar ice, warn of solar storms, forecast Martian weather), then choose the orbit, instruments, power, comms and rocket in a 3D hangar. Every choice costs mass, power, data, money and time. The mission then flies through a physics-based ascent, years of operations and mid-flight crises that a team of four votes on. A debrief explains the result in the player’s own numbers and compares the spacecraft with the real NASA mission that did the same job (Landsat 9, Sentinel-6, Lunar Trailblazer, ACE, MAVEN), with a source for every figure. It addresses the challenge by making mission design (systems thinking, trade-offs, margins) something students do rather than read about. It runs in any browser, in English and Russian, with nothing to install.
details:
What it does. Players walk a mission from brief to debrief: build, development surprises, launch, operations, score. The engine is deterministic: the same seed always replays the same flight, so a four-player team (mission manager, science lead, systems engineer, comms and data) sees the same mission on every device. Each role edits only its own sections and has goals that conflict with the others’.

Realism. Rocket equation, second-by-second ascent, eclipses and battery drain, link budgets. Concept maturity is shown on JPL’s CML 1–4 scale and development as NASA Phases C–D. Catalogue prices and masses were fact-checked against NASA, JPL and ESA pages.

Impact. For students and space clubs without engineering labs: a 20-minute loop of design, fly, read why, change one thing, fly again.

Tools. React, TypeScript, Vite, three.js (planets drawn by shaders), PeerJS/WebRTC, Supabase (optional accounts), Blender (our own 3D models), Vitest (121 tests), Vercel, Canva.
